To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the hyperglucagonemic state of catabolic patients is not a major factor in the increased protein catabolism that is characteristic of such patients.
the hyperglucagonemic state that occurs during stress does not alter protein metabolism in the whole body, but it does stimulate amino acid uptake and extraction by the liver.

the increase in plasma glucagon during the postabsorptive state is not responsible for the increase in leucine proteolysis or the decrease in protein synthesis, nor does it contribute to the increase in net gastrointestinal tract protein loss during the postabsortive state.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of glucagon on protein and amino acid kinetics.
the role of glucagon as a counterregulatory hormone in the catabolic state.
the role of pancreatic hormones in the regulation of whole-body protein and amino acid kinetics in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present study demonstrates that the hyperglucagonemic response to catabolic stress is not a major determinant of protein and amino acids metabolism in vivo.
glucagon is an important regulator of protein and amino-acid metabolism in the liver, but not in the gastrointestinal tract or in peripheral tissues.
the hyperglucagonemic response to stress does not play an independent role in the catabolic response of whole-body protein metabolism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
glucagon does not play a role in protein and amino acid kinetics, or amino acid balance in the liver and gastrointestinal tissues, in conscious, 18-hour-fasting dogs.
glucagon does not play a major role in the control of whole-body protein kinetics in the postabsorptive state.

hyperglucagonaemia per se has no effect on leucine metabolism in the dog, but it does increase amino acid uptake by the liver and decrease the plasma concentration of amino acids, thereby increasing the net hepatic release of amino acids.
The main takeaway from our work is that
glucagon is not a primary regulator of protein metabolism in the postabsorptive state.
hyperglucagonaemia does not contribute significantly to the loss of protein and amino acids during fasting or catabolic conditions.
the hyperglucagonemic state that is present in the catabolic states of sepsis and trauma is not responsible for the increased proteolysis that occurs during these conditions.
